541.event_title: The Supreme Court orders President Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes
541.event: During the Watergate investigation, Special Prosecutor Leon Jaworski subpoenaed tape recordings of conversations in President Richard Nixon's White House, and Nixon refused to hand them over, claiming executive privilege. After hearing argument on 8 July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled 8-0 on 24 July, in an opinion by Chief Justice Warren Burger, that a president's general claim of confidentiality must yield to the demonstrated, specific need for evidence in a criminal trial, with Justice William Rehnquist taking no part. Nixon complied, released transcripts that showed his part in the cover-up, and resigned in August 1974.
541.explanation: The highest court examined the president's claim on its merits and applied the law to the most powerful man in the country as it would to anyone else.
541.tie_back: The kural defines justice as examining the matter carefully, showing favour to no one and deciding with those learned in the law, and the Court's unanimous ruling against a sitting president meets every part of that definition.
541._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of impartial, law-based judgment reaching even the head of state; the kural addresses the king's own justice, here exercised by an independent court.

542.event_title: Hammurabi sets up his law code on a public stela
542.event: Toward the end of his reign, King Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 of his legal decisions, covering matters from prices and trade to family and criminal law, inscribed on a diorite stela set up in a temple. In the epilogue, Hammurabi invites any oppressed person who has a case at law to come and stand before his image, read the inscription and learn what is just. The best-preserved stela was found at Susa in 1901 and is now in the Louvre in Paris.
542.explanation: By placing the law in public view, the king presented justice as something his subjects could look to and rely on, not merely the ruler's private will.
542.tie_back: The kural says the people of a land look to the king's sceptre as living things look to the sky for rain, and Hammurabi's stela explicitly invited every wronged subject to look to the king's justice.
542._accuracy_note: Shows subjects being invited to look to royal justice; the kural's comparison with all life depending on rain is broader than any single act can show.

543.place: Goryeo Korea (the woodblocks are now at Haeinsa Temple, South Korea)
543.event: During the Mongol invasions of Korea, which began in 1231, the Goryeo court under King Gojong undertook to carve the entire Buddhist canon onto wooden printing blocks, in the belief that the Buddha's protection could help drive out the invaders. The work, carried out between 1237 and 1248, produced more than 81,000 blocks. The woodblocks are still kept at Haeinsa Temple, where they are inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register and their storage halls are a World Heritage Site.
543.explanation: In a time of invasion, royal authority and resources preserved a complete body of sacred learning that has survived for nearly eight centuries.
543.tie_back: The kural says the king's rule is the foundation that keeps the scriptures of the sages and the dharma they teach standing, and the Goryeo court used its power to preserve the whole Buddhist canon.
543._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of royal power sustaining sacred texts, matching the modern readings of the kural; it concerns the Buddhist canon rather than the Vedas named by Parimelazhagar.

544.event_title: Thailand honours King Chulalongkorn, the Great Beloved King
544.event: King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) came to the throne of Siam in 1868 and, after his coronation in 1873, carried out sweeping reforms beginning with the abolition of slavery, which was completed by the Slave Abolition Act of 1905, along with new law courts, schools, railways and a system of twelve ministries. He died on 23 October 1910 after ruling for 42 years and became known as Phra Piya Maharaj, the Great Beloved King. The anniversary of his death is a national holiday on which Thais lay wreaths at his equestrian statue in Bangkok's Royal Plaza and at other statues of him, in addition to the flowers that many offer there throughout the year.
544.explanation: More than a century after his death, his people still gather at the feet of his statue, a lasting sign of the affection earned by a ruler remembered for caring for his subjects.
544.tie_back: The kural says the world clings to the feet of the great king who rules while embracing his people, and Thais still gather at the foot of Chulalongkorn's statue to honour him.
544._accuracy_note: A close and almost literal fit to the image of the world clinging to the feet of a king who embraced his people.

545.event_title: Todar Mal's revenue settlement under Akbar
545.event: Under the Mughal emperor Akbar, the revenue minister Raja Todar Mal reorganised the land revenue of northern India. Land was carefully measured, using lengths of bamboo joined with iron rings in place of hemp ropes, and the government gathered ten years of local figures on crop yields and prices to set average rates for each crop in each revenue circle. Under this system, called zabt, the revenue demand was fixed according to the quality of the soil and the continuity of cultivation, at between one-third and one-half of the value of the produce.
545.explanation: Assessing taxes on measured land and long-term average harvests replaced arbitrary demands with a known rule, one reason Akbar's administration is remembered for its order.
545.tie_back: The kural links rule by proper law with abundant harvests, and Todar Mal's settlement shows a government binding its demands to the real yield of the land rather than to the ruler's whim.
545._accuracy_note: No ruler can bring rain, so this is a next-best example of lawful rule bound up with agriculture rather than a demonstration of the kural's claim that just rule brings good seasons.

546.event_title: James II's army melts away in the Glorious Revolution
546.event: James II had alienated many of his subjects through acts such as suspending laws without Parliament's consent and keeping a standing army. When William of Orange landed at Torbay in Devon on 5 November 1688, so many of James's officers deserted, among them Lieutenant-General John Churchill, that James dared not risk a pitched battle, and his own daughter Princess Anne and her husband also abandoned him. Without a major battle, James fled to France in December, and in 1689 the crown was offered to William and Mary together with a Declaration of Rights listing the grievances against him.
546.explanation: A king with a standing army lost his throne almost without a fight, because those who carried his weapons no longer stood behind his rule.
546.tie_back: The kural says it is not the spear that brings a king victory but his sceptre, provided it does not bend, and James II's army was of no use to him once his sceptre had bent.
546._accuracy_note: A strong, near-literal illustration: military force failed a ruler whose people judged his rule unjust.

547.event_title: King Juan Carlos defends Spain's constitution against the 1981 coup
547.event: On 23 February 1981, Civil Guard officers led by Antonio Tejero stormed Spain's Congress of Deputies during the vote to install a new prime minister and held the deputies and members of the government captive for about 18 hours. That night King Juan Carlos appeared on national television to denounce the uprising and call for loyalty to the democratic constitution and the elected government. The coup collapsed, constitutional order was restored, and its leaders were tried and imprisoned.
547.explanation: Because the king stood firmly by the constitution, the lawful order he upheld gave him the authority to stop the coup, and the episode strengthened both Spanish democracy and his own position.
547.tie_back: The kural says the king guards the world and justice guards the king, so long as he upholds it without fail, and Juan Carlos's loyalty to the lawful order protected both his country and his crown in 1981.
547._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a ruler protected by his own adherence to lawful government; later controversies in his life are outside this event.

548.event_title: The Wanli Emperor withdraws from government
548.event: The Wanli Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who reigned from 1573 to 1620, increasingly withdrew from government after the death of his able Grand Secretary Zhang Juzheng in 1582. For years he neglected daily business, failed to appear at court audiences and refused to read the memorials his officials sent him, while factional quarrels among officials grew and more and more of his responsibilities passed to palace eunuchs. Strained by costly wars and an empty treasury, the Ming dynasty fell in 1644, less than a quarter of a century after his death.
548.explanation: Historians commonly trace the Ming dynasty's decline to Wanli's long withdrawal, when officials could no longer reach the throne and the empire's problems went unresolved.
548.tie_back: The kural says a king whom his people cannot reach, and who does not look into their complaints and give justice, sinks low and perishes by his own doing, and the Wanli Emperor's closed court began the ruin of his dynasty.
548._accuracy_note: A close fit to the inaccessible ruler who ruins himself; the dynasty's final fall came after his death and involved rebels and invaders as well.

549.event_title: La Reynie becomes Paris's first lieutenant general of police
549.event: By an edict of March 1667, Louis XIV created the office of lieutenant of police for Paris, bringing together in one office policing duties that had been divided among many officials, and appointed Gabriel Nicolas de La Reynie, who held it until 1697. The office was responsible for public safety, fires and floods, street cleaning, the food supply and public order. Under La Reynie, streets were lit at night by thousands of lanterns and refuse was collected at fixed hours.
549.explanation: The crown treated keeping the capital safe, clean and orderly as a regular duty of government rather than an occasional show of force.
549.tie_back: The kural says guarding the people from harm, caring for them and curbing crime is no blemish on a king but his proper work, and the new Paris police office joined protection, public care and law enforcement in one royal duty.
549._accuracy_note: A good institutional illustration of the kural's three duties of protecting, caring and punishing, though it is an administrative reform rather than a single dramatic act.

550.event_title: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg delivers its verdicts
550.event: After the Second World War, the Allied powers set up the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg to try leading figures of Nazi Germany for crimes including war crimes and crimes against humanity. On 1 October 1946 the judges convicted 19 of the defendants and acquitted 3. Twelve were sentenced to death, three to life imprisonment and four to prison terms of ten to twenty years.
550.explanation: The tribunal held those responsible for mass killing to account through a court of law, with evidence and acquittals, rather than through vengeance.
550.tie_back: The kural compares a king who punishes murderous criminals to a farmer pulling up weeds to save the green crop, and the Nuremberg tribunal removed the chief architects of mass murder so that a peaceful order could grow again.
550._accuracy_note: Illustrates lawful punishment of murderers to protect society; the kural's approval of the death penalty itself is something modern readers and states judge differently.
